turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning. Your partner phoned the rooms, said you had a turn on the train. What brings you in?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Chest. Thought it was a heart attack.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): This morning, and a first time?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. First.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Still tight sitting here?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Your own words, what did it feel like?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Clamped shut, like someone sat on my chest. Shaking like mad. Heart going like a drum.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any pain in the arm or the jaw?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sweaty? Scared?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. Terrified.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Short of breath?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nausea, vomiting, or did you black out?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Cough or fever with it?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Partner said you went pale and they got you off at Rosebank. That right?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long did the whole episode last?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Few minutes. Maybe 10. Then it stopped.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you on any medicines, even from the chemist?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): They mentioned biotene on the phone, and your dad's metaformin.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Sister's, for her hair. Dad's diabetic. His pills, not mine.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): And alcohol?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Weekends. A couple of beers.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): What were you doing just before it started?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Standing. The carriage was packed. I couldn't hear myself think in there.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Been pushing hard at work?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. I've overdone it.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): How do you feel sitting here now?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Like a wet rag. There's a frog in my throat. My feet feel dead.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Feet numb now, or only on the train?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): On the train. Not now.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Earlier you said no to being short of breath.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. Well, actually I couldn't get air. Like breathing through a straw.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm. Chest is clear, heart sounds normal, no murmur, pulse regular.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Working impression is a panic attack, not a heart attack. I'm booking an ECG just now, in the rooms, to be sure.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Ok.

[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll show you a breathing count, in for 4 and out for 6, use it if it starts again. If it happens again before the ECG, come straight back, and go to casualty if the pain stays crushing.

spec.situation: Young adult after a first episode of sudden chest tightness, shaking and fear on a train; thinks it was a heart attack; no drugs; partner phones in details; doctor orders ECG, teaches breathing.

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

features: denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
